questions.q: In the lesson's synchronous example, what is `time.sleep(1)` standing in for?
options: A real network wait — sending a request and waiting for an AI provider's response
A bug that needs to be fixed
A way to slow down the CPU on purpose for testing
A required delay before Python can import requests
questions.explain: time.sleep(1) is a simple stand-in for the real wait that happens during an actual AI API call: time spent waiting on the network and the model, not on your own code.

questions.q: Why does calling three AI APIs sequentially take roughly 3 seconds if each call takes about 1 second?
options: Python runs multiple calls in parallel by default, so it should take 1 second
Network requests always take exactly 3 seconds regardless of how many there are
Each call waits for the previous one to completely finish before starting, so the waits add up
The three() function multiplies the delay automatically
questions.explain: Synchronous code executes one line at a time. Call two cannot begin until call one returns, so three 1-second waits become one 3-second wait overall.

questions.q: What does it mean for a task to be "I/O-bound"?
options: The task requires a GPU to run
The task spends its time waiting on something external (network, disk, database) while the CPU sits idle
The task is impossible to run in Python
The task uses more memory than available
questions.explain: I/O-bound describes work where the bottleneck is waiting on an external resource, not CPU computation — exactly the situation during a network call to an AI API.

questions.q: Why doesn't async help with CPU-bound work, like a tight numerical loop?
options: Async only works with the requests library
CPU-bound work keeps the processor continuously busy, so there's no idle waiting time for another task to use
CPU-bound work can only run on Windows
Async always makes CPU-bound code slower
questions.explain: Async's benefit comes from using idle wait time productively. CPU-bound work has no idle time to exploit — the processor is busy the whole way through, so overlapping tasks doesn't help.

questions.q: What is the core promise of async for the three-API-call example in this lesson?
options: It lets all three slow calls overlap in flight, so the total time approaches the time of the single slowest call instead of the sum of all three
It makes each individual call respond faster
It removes the need for a network connection entirely
It converts I/O-bound work into CPU-bound work
questions.explain: Async doesn't speed up any one call — it lets multiple slow, I/O-bound calls wait concurrently, so three 1-second calls can finish in about 1 second total instead of 3.
